# Memory management

Two scopes: (A) memory behavior of the **operating systems we build** and (B) memory of the **platform services** that build and manage them.

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
## A. On-device memory (generated by the compiler from `memory.profile`)

### A1. Profiles (auto-selected from target hardware when `auto`)
| Setting | low-ram (≤ 4 GiB, kiosks/thin clients) | desktop (4–16 GiB) | workstation (> 16 GiB) |
|---|---|---|---|
| zram size | `min(ram, 4096)` MiB | `min(ram / 2, 8192)` MiB | `min(ram / 4, 8192)` MiB |
| zram algorithm | `zstd` (lz4 on very slow CPUs) | `zstd` | `zstd` |
| disk swap | none | none (no hibernation: kernel lockdown under Secure Boot disables it) | none |
| `vm.swappiness` | 180 | 150 | 100 |
| `vm.watermark_boost_factor` | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| `vm.watermark_scale_factor` | 125 | 125 | 10 (default) |
| `vm.page-cluster` | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| THP | `madvise` | `madvise` | `madvise` |
| `vm.dirty_bytes` / `vm.dirty_background_bytes` | 64 MiB / 16 MiB | 256 MiB / 64 MiB | ratio defaults |
| systemd-oomd | enabled, user slices | enabled | enabled |
| kiosk app `MemoryHigh` / `MemoryMax` | 70% / 85% of RAM | n/a | n/a |

Rationale:
- zram is compressed RAM swap: typical compression 2.5–4× on desktop/browser pages, much faster than disk swap; with zram, high swappiness (> 100, allowed since kernel 5.8) is correct because "swap" cost is low.
- `vm.page-cluster = 0` because zram has no seek cost; reading 1 page at a time avoids decompressing unneeded neighbors.
- `watermark_boost_factor = 0` avoids aggressive reclaim bursts after fragmentation events (smoother on low RAM).
- Absolute dirty byte limits prevent multi-GiB write-back stalls on slow eMMC/USB storage.

Generated `/usr/lib/systemd/zram-generator.conf`:
```ini
[zram0]
zram-size = min(ram / 2, 8192)
compression-algorithm = zstd
swap-priority = 100
fs-type = swap
```

### A2. OOM handling (systemd-oomd + cgroup v2)
- `systemd-oomd` acts on PSI (pressure stall information) *before* the kernel OOM killer thrashes.
- Drop-ins:
  ```ini
  # /usr/lib/systemd/system/user@.service.d/10-oomd.conf
  [Service]
  ManagedOOMMemoryPressure=kill
  ManagedOOMMemoryPressureLimit=50%
  # /usr/lib/systemd/system/-.slice.d/10-oomd.conf  (SwapUsedLimit applies only to units with ManagedOOMSwap=kill)
  [Slice]
  ManagedOOMSwap=kill
  # /usr/lib/systemd/oomd.conf.d/10-foundry.conf
  [OOM]
  DefaultMemoryPressureDurationSec=20s
  SwapUsedLimit=90%
  ```
- Protected services (agent, display manager, kiosk compositor): `ManagedOOMPreference=avoid`, `OOMScoreAdjust=-500`; the agent additionally `MemoryMax=64M`.
- Kiosk: browser in its own scope with `MemoryHigh`/`MemoryMax`; watchdog restarts it on OOM kill and reloads the URL (state loss acceptable for kiosks).

### A3. Boot-time memory
- Initrd < 40 MiB compressed (≤ ~120 MiB unpacked into RAM, freed after switch-root).
- erofs compressed with lz4hc (`Compression=lz4hc` in the usr repart definition) for `/usr`: decompression is cheap and page-cache friendly; compressed pages are decompressed into page cache once.
- Minimum RAM: kiosk 2 GiB, desktop GNOME/KDE 4 GiB (8 GiB recommended).

### A4. Measuring on device (agent inventory, every heartbeat)
`/proc/pressure/memory` (some/full avg10/avg60), `MemAvailable`, zram `mm_stat` (orig_data_size, compr_data_size → ratio), `oom_kill` counter from `/proc/vmstat`, top-5 cgroups by `memory.current`. Fleet console flags devices with `full avg60 > 5` sustained → recommend profile change or RAM upgrade.

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
## B. Platform memory

### B1. Budgets
| Process | Container/VM limit | Target steady RSS | Key controls |
|---|---|---|---|
| api | 1 GiB | 200–400 MiB | `GOMEMLIMIT=900MiB`, streaming bodies, request body caps |
| scheduler | 512 MiB | < 150 MiB | stateless loops, bounded batch reads |
| worker-agent (host) | 256 MiB | < 80 MiB | no artifact buffering; proxies streams |
| build VM | 16 GiB RAM | mkosi + apt + mksquashfs/erofs peaks 6–10 GiB | tmpfs disabled for workspace (use scratch disk) |
| scanner worker | 4 GiB | grype DB (~1 GiB) + YARA compiled rules | process one image at a time per worker; mmap DBs |
| tester | per test VM 2–4 GiB | — | KSM optional for many identical test VMs |
| fleetsrv | 1 GiB | < 300 MiB | batch buffers capped at 5k rows |
| foundry-agent (device) | `MemoryMax=64M` | < 30 MiB | `GOMEMLIMIT=40MiB`, `GOGC=50`, no large allocations |

### B2. Go runtime rules
- Set `GOMEMLIMIT` to ~90% of the cgroup limit (soft limit lets GC work harder before OOM); keep `GOGC=100` on servers, `50` on devices.
- Never `io.ReadAll` artifacts or uploads. Use `io.Copy` with a pooled 1 MiB buffer:
  ```go
  var bufPool = sync.Pool{New: func() any { b := make([]byte, 1<<20); return &b }}
  func copyHashed(dst io.Writer, src io.Reader) (digest [32]byte, n int64, err error) {
      h := sha256.New()
      bp := bufPool.Get().(*[]byte); defer bufPool.Put(bp)
      n, err = io.CopyBuffer(io.MultiWriter(dst, h), src, *bp)
      copy(digest[:], h.Sum(nil)); return
  }
  ```
- Multipart uploads: part size 64 MiB, concurrency 4 → peak buffer ≤ 256 MiB per upload; semaphore across the process caps concurrent uploads (e.g. 2) → ≤ 512 MiB.
- Request size limits: spec JSON ≤ 1 MiB; asset uploads go directly to object storage via presigned URLs, never through api memory.
- JSON decoding of large lists (device reports) uses `json.Decoder` streaming tokens.

### B3. Build VM memory and I/O
- Page cache matters: mkosi reads the package cache repeatedly → keep the package cache on the host NVMe exposed read-only via virtiofs (DAX off) so it is shared across VMs through the host page cache.
- Use scratch disk for the workspace, not tmpfs: images can reach 10+ GiB.
- zstd `--long=27` needs ~128 MiB window per compressor thread; with `-T8` budget ~1.5 GiB.
- erofs build (`mkfs.erofs`) memory scales with file count; ~1–2 GiB for desktop images.

### B4. Postgres
- `shared_buffers` = 25% RAM, `effective_cache_size` = 70% RAM, `work_mem` 16–32 MiB (beware: per sort/hash node per connection), `maintenance_work_mem` 1 GiB.
- pgbouncer transaction pooling: app pools 20/pod; server connections ≤ 200.
- Large tables partitioned (`device_reports`, `audit_log`, `build_events`) so hot indexes fit in memory.

### B5. Redis
- Two logical instances: `cache` (`maxmemory-policy allkeys-lfu`) and `state` (rate-limit buckets, locks; `noeviction`). Never mix — eviction of a lock is a correctness bug.

### B6. Frontend
- Spec in a normalized store (Zustand/Redux), immutable updates with structural sharing; undo stack capped at 200 entries storing JSON Patches (not full snapshots).
- Catalog lists virtualized (react-window) — only visible rows rendered.
- SAT solving and JSON Schema validation in a Web Worker; transfer CNF once (`postMessage` with transferable ArrayBuffer).
- Image assets uploaded with chunked `fetch` streaming to presigned URLs; previews via `createImageBitmap` + downscaled canvas.

### B7. Device agent
- Fixed-size ring buffer (256 KiB) for local log tail; inventory collected incrementally; HTTP client reuses connections; chunk downloads stream to staging file with `pwrite` at offsets and verify per-chunk SHA-256 — memory O(1) in image size.
